question: You are working at a financial institution that stores mortgage loan approval documents on Cloud Storage. Any change to these approval documents must be uploaded as a separate approval file, so you want to ensure that these documents cannot be deleted or overwritten for the next 5 years. What should you do?
options: Create a retention policy on the bucket for the duration of 5 years. Create a lock on the retention policy.
Create the bucket with uniform bucket-level access, and grant a service account the role of Object Writer. Use the service account to upload new files.
Use a customer-managed key for the encryption of the bucket. Rotate the key after 5 years.
Create the bucket with fine-grained access control, and grant a service account the role of Object Writer. Use the service account to upload new files.
explanation: Option A is correct because Cloud Storage Bucket Lock implements SEC Rule 17a-4(f), FINRA, and CFTC compliant WORM storage. Defining a 5-year retention policy prevents any object in the bucket from being deleted or overwritten until it reaches 5 years of age, and locking the retention policy makes it permanently irreversible—even by Project Owners.
hint: To enforce immutable WORM (Write Once, Read Many) regulatory compliance on Cloud Storage objects for a fixed duration (5 years), configure a Bucket Retention Policy and lock it with Bucket Lock.

whyWrong.1: IAM roles like Object Writer control who can upload files today, but a Project Owner or Storage Admin could still modify IAM policies and delete objects later.
whyWrong.2: Customer-Managed Encryption Keys (CMEK) protect data confidentiality at rest and key rotation schedules; CMEK does not prevent authorized users from deleting or overwriting objects.
whyWrong.3: Fine-grained ACLs do not provide irreversible WORM immutability against privileged administrators.

question: Your team will start developing a new application using microservices architecture on Kubernetes Engine. As part of the development lifecycle, any code change that has been pushed to the remote develop branch on your GitHub repository should be built and tested automatically. When the build and test are successful, the relevant microservice will be deployed automatically in the development environment. You want to ensure that all code deployed in the development environment follows this process. What should you do?
options: Have each developer install a pre-commit hook on their workstation that tests the code and builds the container when committing on the development branch. After a successful commit, have the developer deploy the newly built container image on the development cluster.

Install a post-commit hook on the remote git repository that tests the code and builds the container when code is pushed to the development branch. After a successful commit, have the developer deploy the newly built container image on the development cluster.

Create a Cloud Build trigger based on the development branch that tests the code, builds the container, and stores it in Container Registry. Create a deployment pipeline that watches for new images and deploys the new image on the development cluster. Ensure only the deployment tool has access to deploy new versions.

Create a Cloud Build trigger based on the development branch to build a new container image and store it in Container Registry. Rely on Vulnerability Scanning to ensure the code tests succeed. As the final step of the Cloud Build process, deploy the new container image on the development cluster. Ensure only Cloud Build has access to deploy new versions.
explanation: Option C is correct because a production-grade CI/CD pipeline separates Continuous Integration (Cloud Build trigger running unit tests, building container images, and pushing immutable artifacts to Container/Artifact Registry) from Continuous Delivery (a deployment pipeline watching for verified images and deploying to GKE), while revoking direct human `kubectl` deploy permissions on the cluster.
hint: Enforce secure, automated GitOps/CI-CD by using Cloud Build triggers on Git pushes to test and push images to Artifact/Container Registry, followed by an automated CD pipeline granted exclusive GKE deploy permissions.

whyWrong.0: Client-side Git pre-commit hooks run on developer laptops, can be bypassed with `git commit --no-verify`, and require manual human deployment.
whyWrong.1: Requiring developers to manually deploy container images from their workstations after a commit violates automated CI/CD governance and auditability.
whyWrong.3: Container Vulnerability Scanning checks OS/package CVEs rather than running functional unit/integration tests.

question: Your operations team has asked you to help diagnose a performance issue in a production application that runs on Compute Engine. The application is dropping requests that reach it when under heavy load. The process list for affected instances shows a single application process that is consuming all available CPU, and autoscaling has reached the upper limit of instances. There is no abnormal load on any other related systems, including the database. You want to allow production traffic to be served again as quickly as possible. Which action should you recommend?
options: Change the autoscaling metric to agent.googleapis.com/memory/percent_used.
Restart the affected instances on a staggered schedule.
SSH to each instance and restart the application process.
Increase the maximum number of instances in the autoscaling group.
explanation: Option D is correct because the diagnostics confirm that each instance is legitimately saturated by CPU load, downstream databases are healthy, and the MIG autoscaler has hit its configured maximum instance cap (`maxNumReplicas`). Raising the maximum instance count allows the autoscaler to immediately scale out additional VMs to absorb the traffic spike and restore availability.
hint: When a CPU-bound Compute Engine Managed Instance Group drops requests during a traffic spike because autoscaling has hit its configured `maxReplicas` ceiling, immediately raise the maximum instance limit.

whyWrong.0: Changing the autoscaling metric from CPU to memory will not help when CPU is the saturated bottleneck and the group is already capped at `maxReplicas`.
whyWrong.1: Restarting overloaded instances temporarily reduces serving capacity even further, worsening request drops across the remaining VMs.
whyWrong.2: Manually SSHing into instances to restart processes reduces active capacity during an overload event and does not add compute resources.

topic: Infrastructure Provisioning: Network, Storage, Compute & AI
question: You are developing an application using different microservices that should remain internal to the cluster. You want to be able to configure each microservice with a specific number of replicas. You also want to be able to address a specific microservice from any other microservice in a uniform way, regardless of the number of replicas the microservice scales to. You need to implement this solution on Google Kubernetes Engine. What should you do?
options: Deploy each microservice as a Deployment. Expose the Deployment in the cluster using a Service, and use the Service DNS name to address it from other microservices within the cluster.
Deploy each microservice as a Deployment. Expose the Deployment in the cluster using an Ingress, and use the Ingress IP address to address the Deployment from other microservices within the cluster.
Deploy each microservice as a Pod. Expose the Pod in the cluster using a Service, and use the Service DNS name to address the microservice from other microservices within the cluster.
Deploy each microservice as a Pod. Expose the Pod in the cluster using an Ingress, and use the Ingress IP address name to address the Pod from other microservices within the cluster.
explanation: Option A is correct because Kubernetes `Deployments` declaratively maintain the desired replica count and handle self-healing/rolling updates, while a Kubernetes `Service` (default type `ClusterIP`) allocates a stable virtual IP and internal kube-dns name that automatically load balances requests across all healthy Pod replicas.
hint: In Kubernetes, manage replicated stateless microservices using `Deployments` and expose them internally via ClusterIP `Services` so callers address a stable internal DNS name (`<svc>.<ns>.svc.cluster.local`).

whyWrong.1: Kubernetes `Ingress` exposes HTTP/HTTPS routes to external clients outside the cluster, whereas internal east-west pod-to-pod traffic should use `ClusterIP` Services.
whyWrong.2: Deploying standalone naked `Pods` without a `Deployment` controller prevents replica scaling, rolling updates, and automatic rescheduling when nodes fail.
whyWrong.3: Combining naked `Pods` with external `Ingress` resources fails both replica management and internal-only cluster communication requirements.

question: Your company has a networking team and a development team. The development team runs applications on Compute Engine instances that contain sensitive data. The development team requires administrative permissions for Compute Engine. Your company requires all network resources to be managed by the networking team. The development team does not want the networking team to have access to the sensitive data on the instances. What should you do?
options: 1. Create a project with a standalone VPC and assign the Network Admin role to the networking team. 2. Create a second project with a standalone VPC and assign the Compute Admin role to the development team. 3. Use Cloud VPN to join the two VPCs.
1. Create a project with a standalone Virtual Private Cloud (VPC), assign the Network Admin role to the networking team, and assign the Compute Admin role to the development team.

1. Create a project with a Shared VPC and assign the Network Admin role to the networking team. 2. Create a second project without a VPC, configure it as a Shared VPC service project, and assign the Compute Admin role to the development team.

1. Create a project with a standalone VPC and assign the Network Admin role to the networking team. 2. Create a second project with a standalone VPC and assign the Compute Admin role to the development team. 3. Use VPC Peering to join the two VPCs.
explanation: Option C is correct because Shared VPC allows the Networking Team to own and administer the central VPC network in a dedicated Host Project (`roles/compute.networkAdmin`) while the Development Team owns their Compute Engine VMs in an attached Service Project (`roles/compute.admin`). Because the Networking Team has no IAM roles in the Service Project, they cannot SSH into or read sensitive data on the developer VMs.
hint: Shared VPC enforces least-privilege separation of duties: central network admins manage subnets, routes, and firewalls in the Host Project (`roles/compute.networkAdmin`) without having Compute Admin access to VMs in Service Projects.

whyWrong.0: Using Cloud VPN between standalone VPCs adds unnecessary tunnel bandwidth costs and management overhead compared to Shared VPC.
whyWrong.1: Putting both teams in a single project risks privilege escalation or accidental firewall/metadata changes affecting sensitive VMs.
whyWrong.3: VPC Network Peering decentralizes firewall and subnet administration across projects rather than giving the central networking team unified control.

question: Your company sends all Google Cloud logs to Cloud Logging. Your security team wants to monitor the logs. You want to ensure that the security team can react quickly if an anomaly such as an unwanted firewall change or server breach is detected. You want to follow Google-recommended practices. What should you do?
options: Schedule a cron job with Cloud Scheduler. The scheduled job queries the logs every minute for the relevant events.
Export logs to BigQuery, and trigger a query in BigQuery to process the log data for the relevant events.
Export logs to a Pub/Sub topic, and trigger Cloud Function with the relevant log events.
Export logs to a Cloud Storage bucket, and trigger Cloud Run with the relevant log events.
explanation: Option C is correct because Cloud Logging sinks stream matching log entries in near real time to Cloud Pub/Sub, which immediately invokes an event-driven Cloud Function (or Cloud Run service) to alert the SOC or automatically remediate unauthorized firewall changes within seconds.
hint: For real-time event-driven security remediation of Cloud Logging audit/firewall anomalies, route logs via a Log Sink to a Cloud Pub/Sub topic that triggers a Cloud Function.

whyWrong.0: Polling Cloud Logging every minute via Cloud Scheduler introduces up to 60+ seconds of detection latency and unnecessary polling API queries.
whyWrong.1: Exporting logs to BigQuery is ideal for historical forensic SQL analytics, but scheduled BigQuery queries are batch-oriented rather than sub-second event-driven triggers.
whyWrong.3: Cloud Storage log sinks batch log files hourly, introducing high latency unsuitable for real-time security incident response.

question: You have deployed several instances on Compute Engine. As a security requirement, instances cannot have a public IP address. There is no VPN connection between Google Cloud and your office, and you need to connect via SSH into a specific machine without violating the security requirements. What should you do?
options: Configure Cloud NAT on the subnet where the instance is hosted. Create an SSH connection to the Cloud NAT IP address to reach the instance.
Add all instances to an unmanaged instance group. Configure TCP Proxy Load Balancing with the instance group as a backend. Connect to the instance using the TCP Proxy IP.
Configure Identity-Aware Proxy (IAP) for the instance and ensure that you have the role of IAP-secured Tunnel User. Use the gcloud command line tool to ssh into the instance.
Create a bastion host in the network to SSH into the bastion host from your office location. From the bastion host, SSH into the desired instance.
explanation: Option C is correct because Identity-Aware Proxy (IAP) TCP forwarding establishes an authenticated, encrypted HTTPS tunnel from the administrator's workstation to Google's edge and forwards SSH (port 22) traffic to the VM's internal IP address (`35.235.240.0/20`). Users authenticate via IAM (`IAP-secured Tunnel User` / `roles/iap.tunnelResourceAccessor`) without exposing any public IPs or bastion hosts.
hint: Connect via SSH to private Compute Engine VMs (without external IPs or VPNs) using Identity-Aware Proxy (IAP) TCP forwarding (`gcloud compute ssh --tunnel-through-iap`) with the `roles/iap.tunnelResourceAccessor` role.

whyWrong.0: Cloud NAT only translates outbound connections initiated by private VMs to the internet; it does not accept inbound SSH connections.
whyWrong.1: TCP Proxy Load Balancing distributes external client traffic across a pool of backend instances and cannot target interactive SSH sessions to a specific private VM.
whyWrong.3: Deploying a public bastion host requires exposing an external IP address and managing SSH jump-box hardening, which IAP TCP forwarding eliminates.

question: Your company is using Google Cloud. You have two folders under the Organization: Finance and Shopping. The members of the development team are in a Google Group. The development team group has been assigned the Project Owner role on the Organization. You want to prevent the development team from creating resources in projects in the Finance folder. What should you do?
options: Assign the development team group the Project Viewer role on the Finance folder, and assign the development team group the Project Owner role on the Shopping folder.
Assign the development team group only the Project Viewer role on the Finance folder.
Assign the development team group the Project Owner role on the Shopping folder, and remove the development team group Project Owner role from the Organization.
Assign the development team group only the Project Owner role on the Shopping folder.
explanation: Option C is correct because Google Cloud IAM Allow policies are inherited downward from Organization -> Folder -> Project -> Resource. Granting `Project Viewer` on the Finance folder does NOT revoke the `Project Owner` role inherited from the Organization node. You must remove `Project Owner` from the Organization level and grant `Project Owner` specifically on the Shopping folder.
hint: IAM Allow policies in Google Cloud are strictly hierarchical and additive (child resources inherit all parent bindings). To restrict access on a sibling folder, remove the over-privileged role at the Organization root and grant it only on the specific target folder.

whyWrong.0: Because IAM allow policies are unioned down the hierarchy, leaving `Project Owner` at the Organization level ensures the group still inherits full Owner permissions on the Finance folder.
whyWrong.1: Assigning `Project Viewer` on the Finance folder without removing `Project Owner` at the Organization level leaves effective permissions on Finance as `Project Owner`.
whyWrong.3: Failing to remove `Project Owner` from the Organization node leaves the development team with full Owner access across both Finance and Shopping folders.

question: For this question, refer to the Mountkirk Games case study. Mountkirk Games wants you to design their new testing strategy. How should the test coverage differ from their existing backends on the other platforms? (Case Study 1)
options: Tests should scale well beyond the prior approaches.
Unit tests are no longer required, only end-to-end tests.
Tests should be applied after the release is in the production environment.
Tests should include directly testing the Google Cloud Platform (GCP) infrastructure.
explanation: Option A is correct because Mountkirk Games' CEO and CTO explicitly state that previous game launches failed to scale under unexpected player popularity, causing outages and player churn. Their new cloud testing strategy must include automated, large-scale load and stress testing that simulates traffic spikes far exceeding historical peaks to validate autoscaling behavior before launch.
hint: In the Mountkirk Games case study, prior titles suffered severe reputation damage because legacy servers failed under unexpected player spikes; the new testing strategy must validate high-concurrency load and autoscaling well beyond prior limits.

whyWrong.1: Eliminating unit tests violates software engineering best practices and slows down defect detection in microservices.
whyWrong.2: Waiting until after production release to run tests exposes live players to crashes and repeats Mountkirk's past launch failures.
whyWrong.3: Under the Shared Responsibility Model, Google tests underlying GCP hardware/infrastructure; Mountkirk must test their own application code, configuration, and scaling policies.

question: For this question, refer to the Mountkirk Games case study. Mountkirk Games has deployed their new backend on Google Cloud Platform (GCP). You want to create a thorough testing process for new versions of the backend before they are released to the public. You want the testing environment to scale in an economical way. How should you design the process? (Case Study 1)
options: Create a scalable environment in GCP for simulating production load.
Use the existing infrastructure to test the GCP-based backend at scale.
Build stress tests into each component of your application using resources internal to GCP to simulate load.
Create a set of static environments in GCP to test different levels of load -- for example, high, medium, and low.
explanation: Option A is correct because validating an autoscaling game backend requires an elastic staging environment in GCP capable of dynamically scaling under synthetic load generation (e.g., GKE/MIG load generators) and scaling down or being decommissioned when tests complete so Mountkirk only pays for compute consumed during test runs.
hint: For Mountkirk Games' pre-release load testing, spin up an elastic, ephemeral staging environment in GCP that mirrors production autoscaling and tear it down after testing to optimize cost.

whyWrong.1: Mountkirk's legacy physical/leased server infrastructure could not scale to handle previous games and cannot generate or absorb realistic cloud-scale traffic.
whyWrong.2: Embedding load-generation code inside production application components distorts application performance metrics and wastes production compute resources.
whyWrong.3: Maintaining multiple permanent static environments (high, medium, low) incurs continuous idle VM costs and fails to test dynamic autoscaling transitions.

topic: Infrastructure Provisioning: Network, Storage, Compute & AI
question: For this question, refer to the Mountkirk Games case study. Mountkirk Games wants to set up a continuous delivery pipeline. Their architecture includes many small services that they want to be able to update and roll back quickly. Mountkirk Games has the following requirements: Services are deployed redundantly across multiple regions in the US and Europe. Only frontend services are exposed on the public internet. They can provide a single frontend IP for their fleet of services. Deployment artifacts are immutable. Which set of products should they use? (Case Study 1)
options: Google Cloud Storage, Google Cloud Dataflow, Google Compute Engine
Google Cloud Storage, Google App Engine, Google Network Load Balancer
Google Kubernetes Registry, Google Container Engine, Google HTTP(S) Load Balancer
Google Cloud Functions, Google Cloud Pub/Sub, Google Cloud Deployment Manager
explanation: Option C is correct because Container Registry / Artifact Registry stores immutable Docker container images, Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) orchestrates rapid rolling updates and rollbacks across multi-region clusters in the US and Europe, and the Global External HTTP(S) Load Balancer exposes a single global anycast IP address that routes players to the nearest healthy regional frontend.
hint: Mountkirk Games' multi-region microservices CD architecture requires Container/Artifact Registry (immutable images), Google Kubernetes Engine (fast rollouts/rollbacks across US & Europe), and Global External HTTP(S) Load Balancing (single anycast frontend IP).

whyWrong.0: Cloud Dataflow is a streaming/batch data processing engine, not a microservice hosting platform, and lacks a global anycast frontend load balancer.
whyWrong.1: Google Network Load Balancer is a regional Layer 4 load balancer and cannot provide a single global anycast IP spanning both the US and Europe.
whyWrong.3: Cloud Functions and Pub/Sub do not provide a single global frontend IP or multi-region container orchestration.

question: For this question, refer to the Mountkirk Games case study. Mountkirk Games' gaming servers are not automatically scaling properly. Last month, they rolled out a new feature, which suddenly became very popular. A record number of users are trying to use the service, but many of them are getting 503 errors and very slow response times. What should they investigate first? (Case Study 1)
options: Verify that the database is online.
Verify that the project quota hasn't been exceeded.
Verify that the new feature code did not introduce any performance bugs.
Verify that the load-testing team is not running their tool against production.
explanation: Option B is correct because HTTP `503 Service Unavailable` errors paired with an autoscaler that has stopped adding instances during record player traffic is the classic signature of hitting a Google Cloud project or regional quota limit (such as regional vCPU quota or in-use IP address quota). Checking IAM & Admin -> Quotas immediately confirms whether GCP is blocking new VM creation.
hint: When a Managed Instance Group or GKE cluster fails to scale out during a sudden traffic spike and users receive HTTP 503 errors, check regional/project Compute Engine resource quotas (vCPUs, IPs, disks) first.

whyWrong.0: If the backend database were completely offline, all requests would fail immediately rather than the autoscaler failing to provision new game server VMs.
whyWrong.2: While a code regression can increase CPU usage per request, it would not prevent the Compute Engine autoscaler from launching additional VM instances unless quotas or max limits were reached.
whyWrong.3: Speculating about internal load-testing tools ignores the explicit fact that a newly launched feature went viral with record real user traffic.
